section.title: Chapter review and discovery problems
section.p: This chapter began with one small calculation:

The forbidden value h=0 did not stop us from seeing what happens as h gets close to 0. That idea became the language of limits. Limits then gave us continuity, one-sided behavior, infinite behavior, asymptotes, sequences, and two existence theorems.
Before we use limits to define derivatives, it is worth pausing to see the whole map.

subsection.title: The chapter in one picture
subsection.p: A limit is the central idea. The other ideas in the chapter are different ways of asking what a limit is doing.

figure.caption: Limits are the center. Continuity, asymptotes, sequences, and tangent slopes all use the same idea of controlled approach.

subsection.p: The most important habit is not memorizing a table of limit forms. It is asking: What is the input doing, and what target is the output approaching?

subsection.title: A decision guide for limits and continuity
subsection.p: When you face a limit problem, begin with the simplest test. Then move only as far as the problem requires.

table.title: Decision guide for limits and continuity

row.cell: direct substitution gives a real number
Use continuity or the limit laws.
Factor, cancel, expand, combine fractions, or rationalize. Then try again.
left and right sides behave differently
Compute one-sided limits. A two-sided limit exists only if they agree.
Check signs from the left and right. The limit may be \infty, -\infty, or may fail to exist.
Divide by the largest power, or compare leading terms.
an oscillating factor is multiplied by something small
a theorem about continuous functions is tempting
Check the hypotheses first: continuity, closed interval, bounded interval, and the right endpoint information.
Use the \varepsilon-N definition, algebraic limit laws, or monotone bounded convergence.

subsection.p: The warning examples in should stay close by. Most mistakes come from using a true theorem without checking the conditions that make it true.

subsection.title: Review problems
subsection.p: The problems below are grouped by purpose. Some are computational. Some ask for explanations. Some ask for proof. In the proof problems, the goal is not speed. The goal is control.

li.p: Explain the difference between \lim_{x\to a}f(x) and f(a). Give an example where the limit exists but does not equal the function value.
Explain why the condition 0\lt |x-a|\lt \delta appears in the definition of a limit.
What does the statement \lim_{x\to a}f(x)=\infty mean? Why is this not convergence to a real number?
A table gives values of f(x) near x=3, and the values appear to approach 8. Why is the table useful? Why is it not, by itself, a proof?
State the two-sided limit test using left-hand and right-hand limits.
In your own words, explain what continuity at a means.
Why can a removable discontinuity be repaired by changing one value, but a jump discontinuity cannot?
State the Intermediate Value Theorem. Name its main hypothesis.
State the Extreme Value Theorem. Explain why both words closed and bounded matter in the interval hypothesis.
Explain the difference between convergence of a sequence and convergence of a series. Use the words terms and partial sums.

paragraphs.title: C. Reading limits from a graph

figure.caption: Graph for reading one-sided limits, function values, and discontinuities.

li.p: Find \lim_{x\to -1^-}f(x), \lim_{x\to -1^+}f(x), \lim_{x\to -1}f(x), and f(-1).
Find \lim_{x\to 1^-}f(x), \lim_{x\to 1^+}f(x), \lim_{x\to 1}f(x), and f(1).
At which points shown in the graph is f discontinuous? Classify each discontinuity as removable, jump, or neither.
Could changing only f(-1) make the function continuous at -1? Explain.
Could changing only f(1) make the function continuous at 1? Explain.
Find the value of c that makes the function continuous at x=2:
Find the value of c that makes the function continuous at x=2:
Find all points where the function is discontinuous: R(x)=\frac{x+1}{x^2-1}. For each discontinuity, decide whether it is removable or infinite.
Use the Intermediate Value Theorem to show that the equation x^3+x-3=0 has a solution in (1,2).
Use the Intermediate Value Theorem to show that the equation x^5+x-1=0 has a solution in (0,1).
Let f(x)=x^4-4x+1. Explain why f must attain an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum on [-2,3]. You do not need to find them.
The function f(x)=\frac{1}{x} is continuous on (0,1). Does the Extreme Value Theorem guarantee an absolute maximum and minimum on (0,1)? Explain exactly which hypothesis is missing.
A function f is continuous on [0,4], with f(0)=-2 and f(4)=7. What values must f take somewhere on [0,4]? What values might it take, but are not guaranteed by this information alone?
A function g is defined on [0,4], with g(0)=-2 and g(4)=7. But g is not continuous. Can we conclude that g(c)=0 for some c\in [0,4]? Give an example or explain why not.
Give an example of a continuous function on an unbounded interval that has no absolute maximum.

paragraphs.title: E. Proof practice with \varepsilon, \delta, and N
paragraphs.p: These problems are about writing precise arguments. Do not begin by saying it is obvious from the graph. Begin with the error you must control.

li.p: Prove from the definition that \lim_{x\to 3}(2x+5)=11.
Prove from the definition that \lim_{x\to a}(mx+b)=ma+b, where m and b are constants.
Prove from the definition that \lim_{x\to 2}x^2=4. Hint: factor |x^2-4|=|x-2||x+2|. First make |x+2| bounded by requiring |x-2|\lt 1.
Prove from the definition that \lim_{x\to 1}\frac{x^2-1}{x-1}=2. Remember that the definition already assumes x\neq 1.
Prove that \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}=0. Use the precise definition of sequence convergence.
Prove that \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{2n+1}{n+3}=2. Hint: \left|\frac{2n+1}{n+3}-2\right| = \frac{5}{n+3}.
For the sequence a_n=1-\frac{1}{n}, prove directly that a_n\to 1.
Show that the sequence b_n=(-1)^n does not converge. Hint: if it converged to L, the even terms and odd terms would both have to approach L.
Let \varepsilon=10^{-4}. Find a value of N such that n\ge N \Longrightarrow \left|\frac{1}{n}-0\right|\lt 10^{-4}.
Let a_n=\frac{n}{n+1}. Find a value of N such that n\ge N \Longrightarrow |a_n-1|\lt 0.001.

subsection.title: Project: bisection method for a root
subsection.p: The Intermediate Value Theorem proves that roots exist. Bisection turns that proof into a numerical method.
We know p(1)=-1\lt 0 and p(2)=5\gt 0. Since p is continuous, the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees at least one root in (1,2).
The method. Begin with [L_0,R_0]=[1,2]. At each step, compute the midpoint
Then choose the half interval where the sign change remains:
If p(M_k)=0, the midpoint is the exact root and the process stops.

paragraphs.title: Part 1: complete the table
paragraphs.p: Use exact arithmetic or decimal approximations. Keep at least six decimal places in the midpoint and in p(M_k).

paragraphs.title: Part 2: error control
paragraphs.p: After N completed bisections, what is the length of the interval that still contains the root? Start with length R_0-L_0=1. After one bisection, the length is \frac{1}{2}. After two bisections, the length is \frac{1}{4}. Find a formula for the length after N bisections.

paragraphs.title: Part 3: midpoint estimate
paragraphs.p: If the root c lies inside [L_N,R_N], and we report the midpoint M_N=\frac{L_N+R_N}{2}, show that
Use this to decide how many bisections are enough to guarantee an error less than 10^{-4}.

paragraphs.title: Part 4: why continuity matters
paragraphs.p: Construct a function that has f(1)\lt 0 and f(2)\gt 0, but has no root in (1,2). Explain which hypothesis of the Intermediate Value Theorem fails.

paragraphs.title: Part 5: a root without a sign change
paragraphs.p: The function q(x)=(x-1)^2 has a root at x=1, but q(0)\gt 0 and q(2)\gt 0. What does this example show about bisection? Does bisection find every root automatically?

paragraphs.title: Part 6: optional computing
paragraphs.p: Use a spreadsheet or short program to continue bisection until the interval length is less than 10^{-8}. Report the final interval and midpoint. Then graph p(x) near the root and check that the graph agrees with your numerical result.

subsection.title: Discovery problems: secant slopes becoming tangent slopes
subsection.p: The next chapter begins where this one started: with average velocity. The only new step is that we will give the limiting slope a name.
For a function f, a point a, and a nonzero number h, the secant slope from a to a+h is
The derivative will be the limit of this quotient as h\to 0, when that limit exists.
The problems below let that idea appear before its definition.

li.p: Let f(x)=x^2 and a=2. Define m_n=\frac{f(2+\frac{1}{n})-f(2)}{\frac{1}{n}}. Compute m_1,m_2,m_5,m_{10}, and find \lim_{n\to\infty}m_n.

For the same function, define \ell_n=\frac{f(2-\frac{1}{n})-f(2)}{-\frac{1}{n}}. Compute \ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_5,\ell_{10}, and find \lim_{n\to\infty}\ell_n. Do the right-side and left-side secant slopes approach the same number?
Let f(x)=x^3 and a=2. Compute \frac{f(2+h)-f(2)}{h} for h\neq 0, simplify, and then find the limit as h\to 0.
Let f(x)=|x| and a=0. Compute the secant slope for h=\frac{1}{n} and for h=-\frac{1}{n}. Do the two sequences of slopes approach the same number?
Based on the previous problem, explain why the graph of y=|x| should not have a tangent slope at x=0.
Let f(x)=\frac{1}{x} and a=1. Compute and simplify \frac{f(1+h)-f(1)}{h}. Then find the limit as h\to 0.

Choose your own function f and point a. Compute several secant slopes using h=0.1, 0.01, 0.001 and h=-0.1, -0.01, -0.001. Make a conjecture about the limiting slope at a. Then try to prove your conjecture algebraically.

subsection.title: End-of-chapter hook
subsection.p: A limit watches a quantity approach a target. In this chapter, the quantity might have been a function value, a sequence term, or an average velocity.
The next chapter chooses one limit and builds a new object from it:
The numerator measures change in output. The denominator measures change in input. The quotient is an average rate of change. The limit, if it exists, is the instantaneous rate of change.
